Summary: Unleavened bread is eaten through the Passover feast, recalling the haste of the departure from Egypt.
Commandment: Eat unleavened bread throughout the Passover feast.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Unleavened bread recalled bread baked in haste, without time to rise, on the night Israel left Egypt. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).
Function: Flat bread for seven days is a memorial you live with, and that is what makes this ceremonial: a rite of remembrance. Its goal was to keep the haste of the departure from Egypt in front of Israel every year — bread baked without time to rise, eaten all feast week. It did not address a particular evil the way a civil law does; its work was remembrance, not restraint. The bread taught what words alone could not: we left in a hurry, and God brought us out.
